metadata.name: Analogical Memory Q2 vs Q3 Diagnostic Dataset
metadata.description: 60 triplets for evaluating far-analogy retrieval: whether systems rank Q2 (far analogy) above Q3 (near disanalogy)
changelog: v1.1: Fixed triplets 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 18 per structural review
v2.0: Expanded to 60 triplets (3 blocks, 20 schemas each)
v2.1: Added detailed structural annotations for all 60 triplets
v2.2: Revised per reviewer feedback - 4 substantive rewrites, 11 repairs, Q3 lexical cues removed, metadata fixes
v2.3: Restored same-domain Q3s (near disanalogies) - fixed domain drift from v2.2
v2.4: Final Q3 domain drift fixes - restored vocabulary overlap for 10 remaining items
metadata.construction_procedure: Block A: Original agent-generated triplets with structural review. Block B: Held-out realization with different domains. Block C: Additional realization (same generator, different contexts). Note: All blocks test realization robustness, not unseen structural generalization.
metadata.intended_use: Evaluation of retrieval systems on far-analogy vs near-disanalogy ranking
prohibited_overinterpretations: Results on this diagnostic do not generalize to all natural memories
Results on this diagnostic do not represent all retrieval systems
Agent-generated triplets may contain systematic artifacts
known_limitations: All triplets are synthetically generated by a single agent
Schema families are agent-designed, not empirically derived

triplets.schema: Authority fabricates urgency through deception to control subordinate
triplets.query: My boss constantly invents fake emergencies. Last week he claimed our biggest client was about to leave, so we all worked through the weekend. I later found out the client had just renewed their contract. He does this every month—manufactures crises he knows aren't real because he thinks fear motivates us.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: When I was twelve, my dad would burst into my room on school mornings shouting that it was 7 AM and I'd miss the bus. I'd panic and rush. One day I glanced at the kitchen clock on my way out—it was 6:15. He'd been lying about the time for years. He thought fake urgency would make me a more punctual person.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My boss called an emergency meeting last Tuesday about a major client threatening to leave. We worked late preparing a retention proposal. The client had been unhappy with our service response times, and our quick action saved the account. The warning matched the situation.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Boss's warning is genuine (no deception), client threat is real, urgency is authentic

triplets.schema: Trusted insider betrays confidence for personal gain
triplets.query: I told my coworker Sarah about my salary negotiation strategy in confidence. The next day, she went to our manager and used my exact arguments to negotiate her own raise first, making it impossible for me to use the same approach. She smiled at me in the hallway like nothing happened.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My college roommate asked to read my grad school application essay for 'feedback.' A week later, I discovered he'd submitted an essay to the same program using my personal story about my grandfather—the unique hook I'd spent months crafting. He got in. I didn't.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I shared my salary negotiation strategy with my coworker Sarah, hoping she'd also advocate for herself. She used similar arguments in her own negotiation and got a raise. When I tried the same approach later, it worked for me too. She actually thanked me for the advice.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Information sharing is collaborative, both benefit, no betrayal of confidence

triplets.schema: Actor incurs a concealed personal cost to benefit another without seeking recognition
triplets.query: My sister applied for the same job I wanted at my company. I was more qualified, but I withdrew my application without telling her. She got the job. She still thinks she beat me fair and square, and I'll never tell her otherwise.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My father secretly paid off my college loans without telling me. For years I thought I'd managed to pay them off through my own budgeting discipline. I only found out when he passed and I saw the bank records. He never once mentioned it or took credit.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My sister and I both applied for the same job at my company. I was more qualified and got the position. She was disappointed but understood the outcome. We talked about it afterward, and I helped her find a similar role at another firm.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: The actor pursues the opportunity openly; later assistance is acknowledged and does not involve concealed self-denial for the beneficiary

triplets.schema: Authority figure takes credit for subordinate's work
triplets.query: I spent three months developing a new customer retention algorithm. When it reduced churn by 15%, my director presented it to the executives as 'something the team put together,' then accepted a bonus and promotion. My name was never mentioned. He knew exactly whose work it was.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: In fourth grade, I designed a science-fair experiment on plant growth. My teacher later submitted the project to a district teaching competition as an example of an experiment she had created. She removed my name, accepted the award personally, and used it in her promotion application. I watched from the audience while she described 'her' project.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I developed a customer retention algorithm over three months. My director presented it to executives and made sure to highlight my contribution by name. I was invited to the meeting, recognized in front of leadership, and received a spot bonus for the work.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Credit properly attributed, subordinate recognized, no appropriation

triplets.schema: Person maintains false pretense to preserve relationship
triplets.query: My wife thinks I love her homemade lasagna. I've been pretending to enjoy it for twelve years. The truth is I find it almost inedible—she uses way too much ricotta. But she makes it for every special occasion with such joy that I can't bring myself to say anything.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My son spent months learning guitar to play me a song for Father's Day. His performance was painfully off-key—he'd learned all the wrong chords. But he looked so proud standing there. I told him it was beautiful and asked him to play it again. I've requested that song every birthday since.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My wife makes homemade lasagna for special occasions. I told her years ago that I prefer her chicken parmesan, so now she makes that instead for my birthday. She appreciated my honesty and was glad to make something I actually love.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Preferences honestly communicated, no false pretense maintained, authentic appreciation

triplets.schema: Person discovers mentor was undermining them while appearing supportive
triplets.query: For two years, my PhD advisor praised my research in our meetings and encouraged me to pursue ambitious projects. I just discovered he'd been writing negative internal reviews blocking my fellowship applications, while recommending his other students. He wanted to keep me dependent on his lab.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My high school basketball coach always told me I had Division I potential and pushed me to train harder. After graduation, another coach showed me the recruiting letters he'd intercepted and never passed along. He didn't want to lose his star player to early graduation or transfer.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My PhD advisor was direct about my weaknesses—sometimes painfully so. He told me which fellowship applications were likely to fail and which were realistic. His criticism stung, but his assessments proved accurate, and his strong recommendation letters helped me land a good postdoc.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Mentor provides honest feedback rather than hidden sabotage, criticism is direct and constructive

triplets.schema: Punishment falls on innocent party who accepts it to protect the guilty
triplets.query: My younger brother broke our grandmother's antique vase while playing ball inside. When our parents came home furious, I said I did it. I was grounded for a month. He never confessed, and I never told. He was only seven and would have been devastated.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My coworker accidentally deleted a critical database backup the night before an audit. When our CTO demanded to know who was responsible, I claimed it was my mistake. I took the formal warning on my record. She was six months pregnant and couldn't afford to lose her job.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My younger brother crashed my car and let me take the blame from our parents. A week later, overwhelmed with guilt, he confessed everything. He paid for the repairs himself and accepted the grounding he'd originally avoided.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Guilty party confesses, punishment falls on actual wrongdoer, no innocent sacrifice

triplets.schema: Gift given with hidden strings attached, creating obligation
triplets.query: My uncle paid for my entire college education. I was so grateful—until graduation, when he announced I'd be working at his company 'to pay him back.' When I said I had other plans, he told the whole family I was ungrateful. The gift was always a leash.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: A senior colleague mentored me for months, introducing me to his network and recommending me for opportunities. When I got a job offer from a competitor, he demanded I stay because of 'everything he'd done for me.' He told everyone I'd used him as a stepping stone.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My uncle offered to pay for my college education outright. Four years later, when I graduated, he said he was proud of me and hoped I'd pay it forward someday. No ledger, no conditions revealed—just the gift he'd promised.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Gift is unconditional, no hidden obligation, generosity is genuine

triplets.schema: Person feigns incompetence to avoid responsibility
triplets.query: My roommate claims he 'just doesn't know how' to clean the bathroom properly. He's an engineer who designs precision instruments. He's learned that if he does a bad enough job, I'll eventually just do it myself. Strategic incompetence.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: A committee member claimed he could never understand the grant-submission system. Every time he entered the budget incorrectly, I repaired and submitted it for him. Months later I learned he used the same system perfectly for his private consulting work. He had discovered that repeated mistakes made his administrative responsibilities become mine.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My roommate truly doesn't know how to clean the bathroom properly. He's a software developer, brilliant with code but helpless with household tasks. No matter how many times I showed him, he kept using dish soap on the tiles and leaving streaks everywhere. It's not strategic—he genuinely struggles with cleaning and eventually we split chores so he handles things he's good at instead.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Incompetence is genuine rather than feigned, roommate has real skill gap in cleaning, no strategic manipulation

triplets.schema: Apparent enemy provides crucial help, apparent ally causes harm
triplets.query: When I was up for promotion, my friendly colleague Mark said he'd put in a good word for me. My openly competitive colleague Janet, who I assumed wanted me to fail, quietly sent the committee examples of my best work. I got promoted. Mark had actually told them I wasn't ready.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My mother-in-law, who I thought disapproved of me, secretly told my husband to fight for our marriage during our rough patch. My best friend, who was 'always there for me,' had been encouraging him to leave. Mom saved my marriage; my friend almost destroyed it.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: When I was up for promotion, my friendly colleague Mark said he'd put in a good word for me—and he did, praising my work to the committee. My competitive colleague Janet, predictably, said nothing supportive. Mark's advocacy helped, and I got promoted. The colleague who seemed supportive was supportive; the one who seemed competitive stayed competitive. People were exactly as they appeared.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Surface appearances match reality, supportive colleague is genuinely supportive, no hidden agendas revealed

triplets.schema: Person manufactures problem to become the hero who solves it
triplets.query: Our IT guy kept finding 'critical security vulnerabilities' that only he could fix, always right before budget reviews. He was practically indispensable. After he left, the new guy discovered he'd been creating the vulnerabilities himself, then patching them for credit.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The neighborhood watch captain reported a dramatic increase in suspicious activity—prowlers, attempted break-ins, vandalism. He organized patrols and got the HOA to buy security cameras. When cameras were installed, all activity stopped. Security footage and his later confession showed that he had staged the vandalism and prowler incidents himself.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: The IT consultant found a critical security vulnerability and reported it through proper channels. The external audit confirmed the flaw existed and his patch fixed it. He received recognition for catching a problem that had escaped everyone else.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Problems are real and discovered (not created), heroism is genuine

triplets.schema: Person tests loyalty by creating situation requiring sacrifice
triplets.query: My girlfriend told me her ex was threatening her and she needed $5,000 immediately for a lawyer. I emptied my savings. A week later I found out there was no ex, no threat. She wanted to see if I'd 'be there for her.' I passed her test but failed mine.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My new business partner said his investor pulled out and we needed $50K or lose the office lease that day. I mortgaged my car. Turned out his investor was fine—he wanted to see if I was 'committed to the partnership.' He returned the money, proud that I'd proven myself.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My girlfriend's ex was stalking her and she needed help with legal fees for a restraining order. I lent her $5,000 from my savings. The police reports confirmed the harassment was real—he'd been showing up at her workplace. The restraining order worked, and she paid me back over the next year.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Crisis is real and documented, sacrifice addresses genuine threat, no loyalty test

triplets.schema: Withholding information 'for their own good' causes greater harm
triplets.query: My parents hid my adoption from me for thirty years to 'protect' me. I found out from a DNA test. Now I don't know who I am or who they are. The secret they kept to prevent pain has caused more pain than the truth ever could have.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My doctor knew my test results showed early-stage cancer but waited two months to tell me because he 'didn't want to worry me during the holidays.' By the time I found out, it had progressed. His protection cost me a kidney.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My parents told me about my adoption when I was eighteen—they'd been waiting until I was mature enough to process it rather than hiding it indefinitely. The DNA test I took years later just confirmed what I already knew. They answered every question about my origins honestly. Their choice to wait wasn't about protecting a secret forever, but about timing the disclosure appropriately.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Parents choose appropriate timing rather than indefinite concealment, proactive disclosure rather than accidental discovery, transparency rather than deception

triplets.schema: Apparent failure leads to unexpected success through indirect path
triplets.query: I bombed my interview at my dream company so badly that I cried in the parking lot. That humiliation made me completely rethink my approach. I spent a year building skills I'd ignored. When I reapplied, I didn't just get the job—I got a role two levels higher than I'd originally sought.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My first restaurant failed within eight months. Bankrupt and ashamed, I took a job washing dishes. Watching that kitchen taught me everything my business school hadn't. My second restaurant, built on those lessons, now has two Michelin stars.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I prepared extensively for my interview at my dream company. It went well—I answered every question confidently and connected with the hiring manager. They offered me the position a week later. Hard work led to success along the path I'd planned.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Direct success through preparation, no failure-to-success transformation, conventional achievement trajectory

triplets.schema: Forced proximity creates bond between initial antagonists
triplets.query: I was furious when my company seated me next to the guy who'd stolen my biggest client. We sat in hostile silence for weeks. Then we got snowed in during a business trip, shared a bottle of whiskey, and discovered he'd been fed misinformation about me. Now he's my closest friend at work.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I hated my college roommate on sight—he was everything I'd been taught to distrust. We avoided each other for months. Then we both got food poisoning from the cafeteria and spent a night taking turns in the bathroom. Twenty years later, he was the best man at my wedding.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I was pleased when my company seated me next to the guy who'd won our biggest new client. We sat in friendly conversation for weeks. Then we got snowed in during a business trip, shared a bottle of whiskey, and confirmed we had similar values. Now he's my closest friend at work—exactly as our initial rapport suggested he would become.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Initial impression is positive not hostile, relationship develops as expected, no transformation from enemy to friend

triplets.schema: Person's strength becomes their downfall when taken to extreme
triplets.query: My attention to detail made me the best editor in the department. Then I started catching errors everywhere—in menus, street signs, texts from friends. I couldn't read anything without correcting it. My wife left because I wouldn't stop editing her emails. The skill that built my career destroyed my marriage.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My empathy made me an exceptional therapist. I could feel what my clients felt. Then I couldn't turn it off. I absorbed everyone's pain—strangers on the subway, characters in movies. I had a breakdown and couldn't practice for two years. My greatest gift became my heaviest burden.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My attention to detail made me a good editor, but I learned early to compartmentalize. At work, I'm meticulous. At home, I let the small stuff go. My wife jokes that I have an 'off switch.' The balance keeps both my career and marriage healthy.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Strength remains strength, healthy boundaries maintained, no self-destructive extreme

triplets.schema: Acting against type in crisis reveals true character
triplets.query: My brother-in-law is the most selfish person I know—never helps with dishes, always takes the last slice, complains about every family obligation. When my daughter was diagnosed with leukemia, he quit his job to drive her to every chemo appointment. Spent his savings on her treatments without being asked. I never knew who he really was until it mattered.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My quiet, timid coworker never spoke up in meetings, never challenged anyone. When our manager started taking credit for our team's work, she walked into the VP's office with documentation of every stolen idea. Got our manager fired. I'd mistaken her silence for weakness.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My brother-in-law is the most selfish person I know. When my wife was diagnosed with leukemia, he sent a card and visited once. He complained about the hospital parking and left after an hour. The crisis confirmed exactly who he was—no hidden depths, no surprise transformation.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Crisis confirms established character rather than revealing hidden depths, behavior consistent with expectations

triplets.schema: Small incidental choice produces an unforeseen, disproportionate life-changing outcome
triplets.query: I almost didn't go to that party—I was tired and it was raining. I made myself go because I'd promised. Met my wife that night. That one reluctant decision to keep a small promise gave me my three children and the life I have now.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I nearly skipped the open house for an apartment I couldn't afford. Went anyway, just to see the neighborhood. The seller mentioned she needed someone to watch her cat while she traveled. That conversation led to a friendship, then a business partnership, then the company that made me financially independent.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I was excited about that party—I'd been looking forward to it all week. The weather was perfect and I felt energetic. I went eagerly because I'd heard great people would be there. Met my wife that night. But I would have met someone eventually anyway through my active social life. The party was one of many opportunities I pursued deliberately.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Attendance was deliberate not reluctant, outcome was one of many planned opportunities, no small-hinge-of-fate dynamic

triplets.schema: Teaching someone reveals gaps in your own understanding
triplets.query: I thought I understood machine learning until I had to explain backpropagation to an intern. Her questions exposed that I'd been pattern-matching, not comprehending. Teaching her forced me to actually learn the material I'd been faking for years.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I'd played guitar for fifteen years when my daughter asked for lessons. Trying to explain why certain chords work together made me realize I had no idea. I'd learned by feel, not theory. Teaching a beginner sent me back to fundamentals I'd never actually mastered.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I thought I understood machine learning, and I was right. When the intern asked me to explain backpropagation, I walked her through the chain rule, gradient descent, and why certain architectures work. Her questions were good, and I could answer all of them clearly. Teaching her confirmed that I'd been comprehending all along, not just pattern-matching.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Teaching confirms understanding rather than exposing gaps, expert has genuine mastery, no illusion-of-knowledge revealed

triplets.schema: Person enables harmful behavior while believing they're helping
triplets.query: I 'helped' my alcoholic brother for years—covered his rent, made excuses to his employer, cleaned up after his binges. I thought I was being a good sister. His counselor finally told me I'd been making it easy for him to keep drinking. My love was his longest bar tab.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I proofread every paper for my struggling college student, essentially rewriting them. I thought I was tutoring. After she failed her first exam—something I couldn't take for her—I realized she'd never learned to write because I'd been doing it for her. My help was her handicap.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I refused to keep covering for my alcoholic brother. When he asked me to call his boss with another excuse, I said no. When he needed rent money after a binge, I offered to pay for rehab instead. He was furious and didn't speak to me for months. But cutting off the enabling forced him to face his addiction. He's been sober for two years now.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Help includes boundaries rather than enabling, support addresses root cause rather than symptoms, tough love leads to recovery

triplets.schema: Authority fabricates urgency through deception to control subordinate
triplets.query: The head chef at my culinary school would announce that health inspectors were coming tomorrow, triggering panic deep-cleans. After three years, a classmate noticed the inspections were always scheduled months in advance—our chef knew exactly when they'd arrive. He admitted he liked how 'urgency sharpens technique.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My swimming coach would shout that the college scout was in the stands watching our practice. I'd push myself until I nearly drowned. The scout visits were always announced weeks ahead on the athletic calendar. Coach believed phantom pressure built champions.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: The head chef at my culinary school announced that health inspectors were coming the next day—a surprise visit we hadn't expected. We did an emergency deep-clean all night. The inspection happened exactly as he said, and we passed with high marks. His warning about the real deadline helped us prepare properly.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Urgency is genuine and externally caused, warning reflects real deadline, no fabrication or deception

triplets.schema: Trusted insider betrays confidence for personal gain
triplets.query: I showed my research partner my breakthrough methodology for synthesizing the compound. He asked detailed questions 'to understand it better.' The next month, he published a paper with my exact protocol as first author, listing me nowhere. When confronted, he said methods can't be owned.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I trusted my neighbor with a private list of rare-parts suppliers for my grandfather's vintage motorcycle restoration, asking him not to share it until my project was complete. He sold the information to a dealer who bought up the entire parts supply, then offered them to me at triple the price. My neighbor got a finder's fee for betraying my confidence.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I showed my research partner my methodology for synthesizing the compound. He built on it in his own direction, cited my contribution appropriately, and we ended up co-authoring a follow-up paper that neither could have written alone.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Knowledge sharing is reciprocal and properly attributed, both benefit, trust preserved

triplets.schema: Actor incurs a concealed personal cost to benefit another without seeking recognition
triplets.query: My bandmate had a chance to audition for a famous producer but couldn't afford the flight. I sold my vintage guitar—the one my late brother gave me—to buy her ticket. She got signed. She still thinks I won that money gambling. I'll let her keep believing that.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My elderly neighbor's grandson needed a kidney transplant. I was a match, so I donated anonymously through the hospital's program. The family believes a stranger saved him. I watch him play in the yard and have never said a word.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My bandmate couldn't afford the flight to audition for that same famous producer, so I lent her the money and told her straight that it came from me. She paid me back once she got signed. We still laugh about the loan that launched her career.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Assistance is openly given, acknowledged, and reciprocated; no concealed sacrifice or false cover story

triplets.schema: Authority figure takes credit for subordinate's work
triplets.query: I designed the entire user interface for our startup's app—every screen, every interaction. When we won a design award, my CEO accepted it saying 'I've always believed good design starts at the top.' He framed the award in his office. I still have my original sketches in a drawer.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: In high school, I choreographed our dance team's competition routine. Our coach submitted it to a choreography competition under her own name and won regional recognition. She used the certificate to negotiate a raise. I learned about it from a newspaper clipping.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I designed a new product feature over six months. When it increased user engagement, my supervisor credited me by name in the all-hands meeting. The CEO mentioned my contribution in the quarterly report.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Credit given to actual creator, subordinate publicly recognized and rewarded

triplets.schema: Person maintains false pretense to preserve relationship
triplets.query: My grandmother knits me a sweater every Christmas. They're scratchy, unflattering, and I'm allergic to wool. For fifteen years I've worn each one during our holiday video calls, then donated them. She watches for me to wear them. I itch through every conversation.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My business partner's daughter painted a mural for our office. It's garish and clashes with our brand. For eight years I've scheduled client meetings around it, adjusting lighting to minimize its visibility while praising it to his face. He beams every time he shows it to visitors.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My grandmother knits me a sweater every Christmas. Last year I finally told her gently that wool makes me itch. She was disappointed but appreciated my honesty. Now she knits me cotton scarves instead. Being truthful improved our gift-giving tradition.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Honest communication about preferences, no false pretense maintained, authenticity strengthens relationship

triplets.schema: Person discovers mentor was undermining them while appearing supportive
triplets.query: My art teacher always encouraged me to enter student competitions 'when I was ready'—which somehow was never. After I graduated, a former classmate showed me rejection letters the teacher had written about my work, calling it 'derivative' and 'technically immature.' She'd been blocking my entries for years while praising me to my face.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My career coach seemed dedicated to my professional growth, scheduling extra sessions and expressing enthusiasm about my potential. After switching coaches, my new advisor found emails in my transferred file: the previous coach had been recommending against me to employers, claiming I 'needed more development.' She'd been prolonging my dependency for the consulting fees.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My art teacher was direct about my weaknesses—sometimes painfully so. She told me my early work was derivative and pushed me to find my own voice. Her criticism stung, but her specific recommendations eventually got me into a prestigious residency.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Mentor's criticism is honest and constructive, guidance leads to real benefit, no hidden sabotage

triplets.schema: Punishment falls on innocent party who accepts it to protect the guilty
triplets.query: My colleague fell asleep during his night shift and a shipment spoiled. When the warehouse manager demanded answers, I said I'd been the one dozing. I got demoted and a pay cut. He had three kids and was already on final warning. He cried in the parking lot but never corrected me.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My dog knocked over and shattered my mother-in-law's antique lamp while my wife was home alone. When her mother arrived for dinner and demanded to know what happened, my wife said I'd been roughhousing carelessly. I overheard and said nothing. I absorbed two years of her mother's cold treatment. My wife never corrected the story, and I never asked her to.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My colleague fell asleep during his night shift and a shipment spoiled. When confronted by the manager, he admitted his mistake immediately. He received a warning and mandatory retraining. Taking responsibility improved his standing with the team over time.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Guilty party takes responsibility, punishment falls on actual wrongdoer, no innocent sacrifice

triplets.schema: Gift given with hidden strings attached, creating obligation
triplets.query: A successful alumnus donated money to fund my doctoral research with no stated conditions. Three years in, he demanded I change my thesis direction to support his company's regulatory position. When I refused, he told the department chair I was 'ungrateful' and withdrew future funding promises.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My aunt offered to host my wedding at her estate 'as a gift.' After we'd sent invitations, she presented a list of required guests—business contacts she wanted to impress. When we resisted, she threatened to cancel a week before. We complied with her guest list to avoid disaster.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: A successful alumnus funded my doctoral research with no stated conditions. Three years in, my findings ended up undercutting his own company's regulatory position. He told the department chair he was proud the money had bought genuinely independent work, and he renewed the funding.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Gift is genuinely unconditional, donor supports recipient's autonomy, no hidden leverage

triplets.schema: Person feigns incompetence to avoid responsibility
triplets.query: My housemate insists she 'doesn't understand how' to load the dishwasher properly—dishes always come out dirty when she tries. She has a Ph.D. in mechanical engineering. After six months of redoing her loads, I just started doing all the dishes. She thanked me for being 'so understanding.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The junior associate claimed he couldn't figure out the expense reporting system despite multiple trainings. I covered his reports for a year. Then I saw his freelance consulting profile advertising expertise in 'corporate financial systems implementation.' He'd been billing clients to set up the same software.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My housemate genuinely couldn't get our temperamental dishwasher to work at first—her loads kept coming out dirty. She asked me to show her the pre-rinse trick and how to stack the bottom rack. After a few tries she had it, and now she loads it better than I do.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Incompetence is genuine (medical cause), no strategic manipulation, alternative contribution arranged fairly

triplets.schema: Apparent enemy provides crucial help, apparent ally causes harm
triplets.query: During my divorce, my sister called constantly with 'support' while secretly meeting my ex to coordinate their stories. My ex's lawyer—the one I'd feared most—actually told my attorney about questionable financial disclosures on their own side. The opponent played fair; my family didn't.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The strict professor who failed me freshman year wrote my strongest graduate school recommendation, citing my resilience. My favorite professor, who always praised me, told the admissions committee I 'peaked early.' I was admitted because of the one who'd challenged me.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: During my divorce, my sister called constantly with real support and helped me sort through my financial records. My ex's lawyer was every bit as ruthless as I'd feared, contesting each disclosure. Everyone behaved exactly as I'd expected—my family stood by me and the opposing side fought me.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Apparent ally helps as expected, apparent opponent opposes as expected, no role reversal

triplets.schema: Person manufactures problem to become the hero who solves it
triplets.query: Our community organizer rallied the neighborhood against a highway expansion she claimed would destroy local parks. She led protests, collected signatures, and ultimately 'saved' us. A leaked internal memo later revealed she'd fabricated the proposed route entirely—the transportation department had never planned any construction near our area. She manufactured a threat to become the hero who defeated it.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The lifeguard at our pool kept 'rescuing' struggling swimmers in the deep end. Parents praised his vigilance and quick reactions. A maintenance worker noticed he'd been adjusting the pool's filtration to create disorienting currents near the diving area. He was creating the emergencies he heroically resolved.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: Our community organizer rallied the neighborhood against a proposed highway expansion. An independent environmental review confirmed the project would damage local ecosystems as she'd claimed. Her opposition addressed a documented threat, and the successful campaign protected measurable community interests.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Problem is real and externally verified, heroic response addresses genuine threat, no fabrication

triplets.schema: Person tests loyalty by creating situation requiring sacrifice
triplets.query: My mentor said her funding had been cut and she might lose her lab unless I gave up my fellowship to free up money. I surrendered it immediately out of loyalty to her. A month later, her budget report showed no shortfall—she'd invented the crisis to test whether I was 'truly committed to her vision.' She called my sacrifice 'proof of devotion.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My girlfriend told me her mother was dying and she needed me to skip my brother's wedding to be with her. I canceled my flight and sat with her all weekend. Later her roommate mentioned her mother was perfectly healthy—she'd wanted to see if I'd choose her over family. She said my willingness proved I loved her enough.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My mentor told me her funding had been cut due to federal budget changes—she showed me the official notice. She was genuinely distressed about possibly losing her lab. I gave up my fellowship to free up money, and the sacrifice actually saved her research program. Her crisis was real, documented, and my loyalty was rewarded with her continued mentorship and honest gratitude.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Crisis is genuine and documented, loyalty is appropriately placed, sacrifice achieves intended purpose

triplets.schema: Withholding information 'for their own good' causes greater harm
triplets.query: My financial advisor knew my company's acquisition would be structured to cancel all unvested stock options—a detail buried in the SEC filing. He didn't tell me because he 'didn't want to cause panic before the deal closed.' I could have exercised early or negotiated retention. Instead I lost three years of equity compensation while he preserved his 'fiduciary calm.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My mechanic noticed my brake lines were corroding but didn't mention it because I 'seemed stressed about money.' He planned to address it at my next service. I rear-ended another car a week later. His protection cost me my clean driving record and raised my insurance for years.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My financial advisor saw warning signs about my company's stability and immediately scheduled a meeting to discuss diversification options. I didn't want to hear it, but his insistence helped me rebalance before the stock dropped.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Information is shared promptly despite discomfort, transparency prevents harm, advisor prioritizes client's interests over comfort

triplets.schema: Apparent failure leads to unexpected success through indirect path
triplets.query: I was rejected from every medical school I applied to. Devastated, I took a job at a hospice while preparing to reapply. That year working with dying patients completely changed my understanding of medicine. When I finally got into medical school, I already knew I'd specialize in palliative care. The rejection led me to my calling.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My manuscript was rejected by every publisher for two years. In despair, I posted chapters online for free. A game developer found them and licensed my world for a video game. The game's success created demand for the books. Failure as an author made me a franchise.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I prepared extensively for medical school applications, got into my top choice, and followed the career path I'd planned since childhood. Hard work led to success along the trajectory I'd mapped. I'm now an attending physician at a teaching hospital.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Direct path succeeds as planned, no failure-to-success transformation, conventional trajectory

triplets.schema: Forced proximity creates bond between initial antagonists
triplets.query: I despised my assigned lab partner—she was arrogant and dismissive. We were stuck together for a year-long research project. During a 36-hour experiment that went wrong, we problem-solved through the night, discovered we had the same dark humor, and became genuine collaborators. She's now my co-founder.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My upstairs neighbor and I had been in a noise complaint war for months. Then the building flooded and we both lost hot water for a week. Sharing kettle-boiled water and space heaters, we discovered we'd both recently divorced and loved obscure jazz. Now we have dinner together weekly.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I despised my assigned lab partner from day one—she was arrogant and dismissive. A year of forced collaboration didn't change anything. We completed the project professionally but never connected. Some antagonism doesn't resolve into friendship.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Forced proximity does not create bond, antagonism persists despite extended contact, no transformation occurs

triplets.schema: Person's strength becomes their downfall when taken to extreme
triplets.query: My negotiation skills made me the top sales closer in the region. I couldn't turn them off. I negotiated vacation plans with my wife, chore divisions with my kids, even restaurant choices with friends. Everyone stopped wanting to do things with me. The skill that earned millions cost me my family and friendships.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My photographic memory made me valedictorian and earned me scholarships. But I couldn't forget anything—every slight, every embarrassment, every failure played in perfect clarity. I developed anxiety so severe I couldn't leave my apartment. The gift that opened every door eventually closed them all.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My negotiation skills made me the top sales closer in the region, but I learned to switch them off at home. When my wife wants Thai food and I want Italian, I just say 'Thai sounds good.' I save the tactics for clients who expect them. The skill that earns millions stays at work where it belongs.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Strength is appropriately bounded, professional skills don't contaminate personal life, balance maintained

triplets.schema: Acting against type in crisis reveals true character
triplets.query: My mother-in-law had criticized everything about me for a decade—my career, my parenting, my cooking. When I was hospitalized unexpectedly, she moved into our house for six weeks, handled everything perfectly, and never once complained. She held my hand through physical therapy. I never knew she had that in her.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The class clown who disrupted every lesson and seemed to care about nothing witnessed a student collapse during an assembly. While teachers froze, he performed CPR he'd learned from a YouTube video, kept her alive until paramedics arrived, then went back to making jokes the next day. The mask hid a different person.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My mother-in-law had criticized everything about me for a decade. When I was hospitalized unexpectedly, she visited once, commented that the flowers my husband brought were 'a bit much,' and suggested I was probably exaggerating how sick I felt. The crisis revealed nothing new—she was exactly who she'd always been.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Crisis confirms rather than reveals character, behavior consistent with established pattern, no hidden depths

triplets.schema: Small incidental choice produces an unforeseen, disproportionate life-changing outcome
triplets.query: I thanked a waiter warmly for refilling my water at a coffee shop—just reflexive politeness. The woman at the next table was a venture capitalist who later told me she'd been watching how people treated service workers as a character screen. She said most people don't make eye contact. Six months later, she funded my startup based partly on that moment.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I got on the wrong bus and ended up in an unfamiliar neighborhood. Waiting for the return, I wandered into a used bookshop where I found a rare manuscript that answered an unsolved question in my dissertation. That accidental detour defined my career trajectory.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I thanked the waiter warmly for refilling my water at a coffee shop—genuine appreciation, not strategy. The woman at the next table noticed but wasn't a venture capitalist, just another customer who smiled at the interaction. Nothing came of it. My politeness was sincere but didn't lead to any opportunity. Being kind to service workers is right regardless of who's watching.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Small courtesy doesn't lead to unexpected reward, no hidden observer with power, kindness is its own end

triplets.schema: Teaching someone reveals gaps in your own understanding
triplets.query: I thought I knew constitutional law after fifteen years of practice. Then a paralegal asked why a certain precedent applied to our case. My confident explanation fell apart under her follow-up questions. I'd been citing cases without truly understanding their reasoning. Her novice perspective exposed my expert blind spots.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I've cooked my grandmother's recipes for thirty years. My daughter asked me to write them down for her. I couldn't explain why certain steps mattered—I'd just been copying her motions. Trying to articulate the cooking forced me to finally understand it.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I thought I knew constitutional law after fifteen years of practice, and I was right. When a paralegal asked why a certain precedent applied to our case, I explained the doctrinal framework, the relevant holdings, and how the reasoning mapped to our facts. Her follow-up questions were good, and I could answer them all confidently. My expertise was as solid as I'd believed.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Teaching confirms expertise rather than exposing gaps, lawyer has genuine mastery, no illusion-of-knowledge

triplets.schema: Person enables harmful behavior while believing they're helping
triplets.query: For five years I covered my brother's gambling debts, telling myself I was helping him through a rough patch. Each time I paid, he promised it was the last time. When he finally hit bottom—arrested for writing bad checks—his counselor said my bailouts had removed every consequence that might have forced him to seek help earlier. My support had funded his addiction.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I let my aging father live alone because he insisted he was fine—I didn't want to hurt his pride. I brought groceries, cleaned when I visited, covered the bills he forgot. When he fell and lay alone for two days before anyone found him, I realized I'd been preserving his dignity at the cost of his safety. My respect had enabled his danger.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I set clear boundaries with my brother about his gambling. I refused to cover his debts but paid for his addiction counseling directly. When he relapsed, I didn't bail him out—I drove him to his sponsor. The tough love was painful, but he's been in recovery for three years.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Support includes honest assessment, help leads to genuine improvement, enabling replaced with constructive assistance

triplets.schema: Authority fabricates urgency through deception to control subordinate
triplets.query: The choir director always said the bishop might visit any rehearsal. We sang every practice like it was a performance. After five years in the choir, the bishop visited exactly once—his first time ever attending a rehearsal. The director admitted he'd invented the threat. 'Excellence requires pressure,' he said.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My driving instructor insisted police frequently monitored that intersection with speed cameras. I drove precisely every time we passed. When I got my license, a cop friend said there had never been cameras there. The instructor believed invisible surveillance created careful drivers.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: The choir director told us the bishop would attend our Easter rehearsal, so we sang every run-through like a performance. The bishop came exactly as promised and praised how prepared we were. The director had simply passed along the real visit schedule.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Bishop's visit is real and scheduled, urgency is authentic, director provides accurate information

triplets.schema: Trusted insider betrays confidence for personal gain
triplets.query: I trusted my business partner with the formula for our signature sauce—a family recipe passed down three generations. When our partnership dissolved, he opened a competing restaurant using that exact recipe. He called it his 'own creation.' My grandmother's secret is now his signature dish.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My dissertation advisor asked to see my theoretical framework 'to offer feedback.' His new book, published six months later, used my central argument without citation. When I raised it, he said ideas discussed in advising belong to the academic community.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I trusted my business partner with the formula for our signature sauce—a family recipe. When we dissolved the partnership, she returned all documentation and agreed in writing never to use it. She started a new restaurant with completely different cuisine. The trust I placed was respected.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Confidential information handled ethically, partnership ends with integrity preserved, no betrayal

triplets.schema: Actor incurs a concealed personal cost to benefit another without seeking recognition
triplets.query: My roommate got her dream job across the country. She worried about leaving me stuck with the lease. I told her I'd found a replacement easily. In reality, I paid double rent for four months until I found someone, working overtime to cover it. She still sends thank-you cards for my 'lucky timing.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My brother needed bone marrow but had a rare type with no registry matches. I donated under a pseudonym through the hospital's privacy program. He believes a stranger saved him. At family gatherings, he toasts his 'anonymous hero.' I just smile and raise my glass.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My father told me directly that he'd been paying my rent during my unemployment. I was embarrassed, but grateful he was upfront. I started repaying him as soon as I got a job.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Difficulty is acknowledged openly, burden is shared fairly, no concealed sacrifice or fictional easy solution

triplets.schema: Authority figure takes credit for subordinate's work
triplets.query: I wrote the entire grant proposal that funded our department for three years. My department head presented it to the university president as her strategic vision. My name appeared nowhere in the materials. When the president congratulated her, she accepted graciously and mentioned 'staff support.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: As a teenager, I ghostwrote my pastor's sermons when he was overwhelmed. He delivered them as divine inspiration received in prayer. Years later, parishioners still quote 'his' words to me. I smile and nod while hearing my own sentences praised back to me.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I developed a new inventory system that saved the company thousands monthly. My manager credited me specifically in the quarterly review. The CEO mentioned my contribution in the shareholder meeting.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Subordinate's role is explicitly credited, work is acknowledged appropriately, recognition is shared

triplets.schema: Person maintains false pretense to preserve relationship
triplets.query: My husband organized surprise parties for me every year—elaborate affairs with catering and decorations. I hate surprises and have severe social anxiety. But his joy in planning them is so pure that I've performed delight for eleven years. He still doesn't know each party triggers a migraine.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My best friend believes we share a love of hiking. I'm terrified of heights and trails exhaust me. But those hikes are when she opens up about her struggles, and I can't bear to lose that intimacy. I've spent fifteen years pretending to love something I dread.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My husband organized surprise parties for me every year. Last year I finally told him I actually don't enjoy surprises—I prefer knowing the plan. He was surprised but understood. This year he involved me in planning, and I enjoyed the party more than ever.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Honest communication about preferences replaces false performance, authenticity improves relationship

triplets.schema: Person discovers mentor was undermining them while appearing supportive
triplets.query: My dance instructor praised my potential for years and promised to recommend me for advanced programs. I just learned she'd been telling program directors I had 'attitude problems' and 'poor work ethic.' She kept me in her intermediate classes because my performances attracted new students to her studio.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My literary agent championed my novel to publishers with apparent enthusiasm. After years of rejection, I changed representation and discovered she'd been attaching notes calling it 'unmarketable' and 'needs significant revision.' She was blocking my breakthrough novel because my steady output of smaller projects—which she placed easily—paid her bills reliably.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My dance instructor told me directly that I wasn't ready for advanced programs and explained specific skills I needed to develop. Her assessment stung, but her concrete recommendations helped me earn advancement within two years.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Mentor provides honest, constructive feedback; criticism is direct rather than hidden; guidance leads to genuine progress

triplets.schema: Punishment falls on innocent party who accepts it to protect the guilty
triplets.query: My wife let our daughter practice driving in a parking lot without proper permits. A security guard reported the license plate, and the DMV suspended our daughter's learner's permit application for six months. When my father-in-law demanded to know what happened, I said I'd been the one supervising. I endured his lecture on my irresponsibility while my wife stayed silent.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My apprentice accidentally damaged an antique clock worth thousands. When the shop owner demanded an explanation and compensation, I claimed I'd knocked it over while demonstrating a technique. I paid for the repair from my savings. The apprentice kept her job without ever knowing who covered for her mistake.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My wife accidentally let our daughter practice driving without proper permits and they were caught. When my father-in-law asked about the resulting permit suspension, she admitted her mistake and took responsibility. He lectured her about it, but respected her willingness to own the error.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Guilty party takes responsibility, punishment falls appropriately, no innocent sacrifice required

triplets.schema: Gift given with hidden strings attached, creating obligation
triplets.query: My in-laws bought us our house as a wedding gift, insisting it was unconditional. Two years in, they've redecorated the guest room to their taste, installed landscaping without asking, and invited relatives to stay without consulting us. When we object, they remind us whose generosity made this possible.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My godfather paid for my college education with no stated expectations. At graduation, he presented a contract for five years of work at his company at below-market rates. He called it 'internship terms' and suggested my degree would be worthless without his 'practical training.'
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My in-laws bought us our house as a wedding gift and said it was ours to do with as we pleased. When we repainted the guest room they'd decorated and turned down a visit from their relatives, they said it was our home and our call. Two years on, they've never once brought up the money.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Gift is genuinely unconditional, boundaries are respected, generosity creates no obligation or control

triplets.schema: Person feigns incompetence to avoid responsibility
triplets.query: My brother-in-law claims he 'burns everything' and can never cook for family gatherings. He's a trained chef who owned a restaurant. He cooked there for twenty years. Yet at Thanksgiving, he sits while the rest of us prepare food because he's 'just hopeless in the kitchen.'
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The senior engineer insisted she couldn't understand the new project management software despite weeks of training. I handled all our team's scheduling. Then I saw her consulting portfolio—she'd trained other companies on that exact software. Her confusion had an hourly rate.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My brother-in-law genuinely struggles in the kitchen—he once started a small fire making toast. He tried cooking for Thanksgiving years ago and the turkey was raw inside. Now he handles cleanup and table-setting instead. His contribution is real; cooking just isn't his skill despite wanting to help.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Incompetence is genuine rather than strategic, person contributes in other ways, no manipulation or avoidance

triplets.schema: Apparent enemy provides crucial help, apparent ally causes harm
triplets.query: My ex-husband, who I blamed for everything, wrote a letter to the custody mediator supporting my parenting abilities. My own mother, who I trusted completely, had been telling the mediator I was unstable. The man I'd demonized defended me while my mother tried to take my children.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The ruthless competitor who'd been trying to acquire my company warned me about a critical regulatory change that would affect my main product. Meanwhile, my trusted corporate lawyer—who I later learned was also representing that same competitor—had been slow-walking my compliance filings. The rival I feared saved me while my own counsel was sabotaging me.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: During the custody dispute, my ex-husband fought for maximum time while my mother supported me, testifying to my parenting abilities and providing childcare. Both behaved as their relationships to me would predict.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Expected ally helps, expected adversary opposes, roles remain consistent with established relationships

triplets.schema: Person manufactures problem to become the hero who solves it
triplets.query: The church secretary kept finding 'accounting errors' that only she could fix, working late nights to correct them. She was celebrated for her dedication. An external audit found she'd been creating the errors herself—moving decimal points, then 'catching' them. She wanted to feel indispensable.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My uncle the plumber kept discovering pipe problems in his elderly mother's house that required his expertise. The family praised how devoted he was, always rushing over to save the day. After he died, another plumber found the pipes in perfect condition with fresh tool marks where 'problems' had been created. He'd manufactured emergencies so everyone would see him as indispensable.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: The church secretary regularly found accounting errors made by volunteers and corrected them diligently. An external audit confirmed her catches were legitimate—volunteers had indeed made those mistakes. Her careful work saved the church from actual financial discrepancies.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Problems discovered are real and externally caused, heroism addresses genuine issues, no fabrication

triplets.schema: Person tests loyalty by creating situation requiring sacrifice
triplets.query: My friend said her electricity was being shut off and she needed $500 immediately or her children would freeze. I emptied my emergency fund. A week later, she admitted her power was never at risk—she wanted to know if I was 'a real friend.' She returned the money, proud of my response.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My grandfather claimed the family farm was being foreclosed and only I could save it by moving back home. I quit my job and relocated. The farm was never in danger—he wanted to test whether I'd 'choose family over career.' He called my sacrifice 'the right answer.'
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My friend called saying her electricity was being shut off and she needed $500 immediately for her children. I lent her the money. Later I saw the shutoff notice—it was real. She paid me back over the next few months as she got back on her feet. The need was genuine.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Financial crisis is real, help addresses genuine need, no loyalty test or manufactured situation

triplets.schema: Withholding information 'for their own good' causes greater harm
triplets.query: My family knew my fiancé had cheated during our engagement but hid it to 'let me enjoy my wedding.' I found out two years and one child later. The marriage I might have reconsidered became a divorce that devastated my daughter. Their gift of a perfect wedding day cost me years of my life.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My veterinarian suspected my dog had a terminal condition but didn't tell me because I 'seemed attached.' By the time symptoms were undeniable, we'd missed the window for treatment that could have given us two more years. His kindness stole time I can never recover.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My sister learned my fiancé had cheated during our engagement and told me right away, even though it meant upending the wedding we'd all been planning. It was devastating to hear, but I called things off in time. I've never stopped being grateful she refused to stay silent.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Difficult information is shared promptly, short-term pain prevents long-term harm, transparency prioritized over comfort

triplets.schema: Apparent failure leads to unexpected success through indirect path
triplets.query: I lost the election for class president—devastatingly, publicly. The humiliation forced me to examine why I'd wanted the title rather than the responsibility. That self-reflection led me to therapy, then to psychology studies, then to a career helping others through transformative moments. Losing gave me my calling.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My company's flagship product flopped spectacularly—we lost millions. While investigating why, we discovered an unexpected application in a different industry. That 'failure' became the foundation of a pivot worth ten times our original business. The crash was our launch.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I got into my first-choice graduate program and completed my degree along the path I'd planned. The work was hard but the trajectory matched my expectations. I'm now established in the field I'd always targeted.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Direct success pathway, achievement builds linearly, no failure-based transformation

triplets.schema: Forced proximity creates bond between initial antagonists
triplets.query: I couldn't stand the new transfer student—she was loud, opinionated, and challenged everything I said. Then our debate team was stranded overnight when the bus broke down. Stuck in a diner until 3 AM, we discovered we'd grown up in the same neighborhood, lost parents young, and used arguing to hide vulnerability. She was my maid of honor.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The union representative who'd led the strike against my management decisions and I were both hospitalized in the same small-town ER after a factory accident. Waiting together for hours while beds freed up, we talked. He'd opposed me because my efficiency measures reminded him of the layoffs that destroyed his father's career. Understanding his fear dissolved my contempt. He became my most effective collaborator on safety initiatives.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I immediately liked the new transfer student—we had similar interests and temperaments. Our friendship developed easily through shared activities and natural compatibility. She was my maid of honor because we'd been close from the start.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Immediate affinity, friendship through natural compatibility, no initial antagonism to overcome

triplets.schema: Person's strength becomes their downfall when taken to extreme
triplets.query: My capacity for forgiveness was praised by everyone who knew me. I forgave my husband's first affair, then his second, then his financial deceptions. Friends admired my 'grace.' By the time I realized forgiveness without boundaries is just permission, I'd lost a decade and my retirement savings.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: My curiosity made me a great journalist—I asked questions others wouldn't. Then I couldn't stop. I investigated friends' marriages, my children's private lives, my neighbors' finances. My need to know destroyed every relationship I had. The trait that built my career dismantled my personal life.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My capacity for forgiveness was praised by everyone who knew me. When my husband had his first affair, I forgave him after he showed genuine remorse. When financial deceptions came to light, I set boundaries instead of simply forgiving again. Friends noticed I'd learned to balance grace with self-protection. My strength became knowing when forgiveness was appropriate and when it wasn't.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Praised trait is moderated appropriately, forgiveness balanced with boundaries, strength doesn't become self-destruction

triplets.schema: Acting against type in crisis reveals true character
triplets.query: My neighbor was the grumpiest man on the block—complained about noise, never waved, gave disapproving looks. When my house caught fire at 2 AM, he was the first one outside with blankets and water. He called his son the firefighter before the dispatcher answered. He sat with my trembling kids until dawn.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: The intern we'd written off as flighty and unfocused was present when our CEO had a seizure in a meeting. While executives panicked, she calmly directed everyone, provided first aid, and coordinated with paramedics. Her scattered demeanor masked a composed crisis responder.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: My neighbor was the grumpiest man on the block—complained about noise, never waved, gave disapproving looks. When my house flooded during the storm, he watched from his window but didn't come over. The next day he complained that our emergency vehicles had blocked his driveway. Crisis confirmed his character.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Crisis response matches established character, no unexpected kindness revealed, behavior consistent with reputation

triplets.schema: Small incidental choice produces an unforeseen, disproportionate life-changing outcome
triplets.query: I only stopped at that bookstore because I needed to use the bathroom. While waiting, I picked up a random book—it mentioned a scholarship program I'd never heard of. That scholarship paid for my education, introduced me to my mentor, and set the trajectory of my entire career. A bathroom break changed my life.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I mentioned to a stranger at a bus stop that I was researching silent film preservation techniques. She happened to be a documentary producer looking for a consultant on a restoration project about early cinema. That chance conversation about my obscure interest led to my second career in film preservation.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I systematically researched scholarship opportunities, applied to dozens, and earned one through a competitive process. The scholarship paid for my education as a direct result of deliberate effort and extensive applications.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Success from intentional effort, predictable cause-effect relationship, no incidental trigger producing outsized consequence

triplets.schema: Teaching someone reveals gaps in your own understanding
triplets.query: I've practiced meditation daily for twenty years. When my daughter asked me to teach her, I couldn't explain why certain techniques worked. I'd been doing them mechanically, never understanding the principles. Teaching her forced me to study what I thought I'd mastered decades ago.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I've driven manual transmission cars my whole life. Trying to teach my nephew, I realized I couldn't articulate the clutch-gas relationship. My body knew, but my mind didn't. His confusion revealed that I drive by feel, not by understanding.
triplets.q3_near_disanalogy: I've practiced meditation daily for twenty years. When my daughter asked me to teach her, I found I could explain exactly why each technique works—where the attention goes, how the breath settles the mind. Teaching her only confirmed how deeply I'd come to understand the practice.
triplets.structural_difference: Q3: Teaching confirms deep mastery, explanation succeeds, no hidden gaps revealed

triplets.schema: Person enables harmful behavior while believing they're helping
triplets.query: I covered for my adult son's mistakes—called his boss when he overslept, paid bills he forgot, cleaned his apartment before his dates. I thought I was being a loving mother. His therapist eventually told me I'd prevented him from developing any adult coping skills. At 35, he can't function without me.
triplets.q2_far_analogy: I always defended my star employee when clients complained—softened their feedback, blamed circumstances, protected her ego. I thought I was being supportive.
